claim: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) are the most prescribed medications for major depressive episodes.
source: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) are the most prescribed medications for major depressive episodes (Bauer et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2008

claim: The effects of SSRI on improving mood and reducing anxiety have been well documented.
source: The effects of SSRI on improving mood and reducing anxiety have been well documented (Trivedi et al., 2006; Stahl, 2008; Cipriani et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Trivedi et al., 2006; Stahl, 2008; Cipriani et al., 2009

claim: Serotonin modulates emotional processing even in healthy volunteers.
source: many experimental studies showed that serotonin modulates emotional processing even in healthy volunteers (Harmer et al., 2009; Serretti et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harmer et al., 2009; Serretti et al., 2010

claim: Loss of interest or pleasure in daily activities is a key symptom of depression.
source: Loss of interest or pleasure in daily activities is also a key symptom of depression (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to American Psychiatric Association, 2013

claim: The impact of SSRI on the motivation deficit (apathy) remains rather controversial.
source: However, the impact of SSRI on the motivation deficit (apathy) remains rather controversial (Papakostas et al., 2006; Weber et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Papakostas et al., 2006; Weber et al., 2009

claim: SSRI treatments do not reduce apathy as much as other symptoms.
source: several studies reported that SSRI treatments do not reduce apathy as much as other symptoms (Fava et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fava et al., 2014

claim: SSRI can induce apathy in patients.
source: or can even induce apathy in patients (Barnhart et al., 2004; Sansone and Sansone, 2010; Padala et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barnhart et al., 2004; Sansone and Sansone, 2010; Padala et al., 2012

claim: SSRI treatments increase motivation or at least the sensitivity to reward.
source: However, other studies also reported that SSRI treatments increase motivation or at least the sensitivity to reward (Tang et al., 2009; Stoy et al., 2012; Yuen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang et al., 2009; Stoy et al., 2012; Yuen et al., 2014

claim: Some studies on cost/benefit trade-off showed reduced effort expenditure with SSRIs.
source: some studies on cost/benefit trade-off showed reduced effort expenditure with SSRIs (Yohn et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yohn et al., 2016

claim: Serotonin blockers have no effect on effort expenditure in cost/benefit trade-off tasks.
source: or no effect with serotonin blockers (Denk et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Denk et al., 2005

claim: SSRI increases motor activity.
source: while other studies reported increased motor activity induced by SSRI (Weber et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weber et al., 2009

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus increases motor activity.
source: or optogenetic stimulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus (Warden et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warden et al., 2012

claim: SSRI treatment decreases apathy in late-life depression.
source: an SSRI treatment was reported to decrease apathy in late-life depression (Yuen et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yuen et al., 2014

claim: SSRI treatment increases apathy in Parkinson's disease.
source: and to increase it in Parkinson's disease (Zahodne et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zahodne et al., 2012

claim: Serotonin is implicated in the motor aspects of action production.
source: Previous studies suggested that serotonin is implicated in the motor aspects of action production and also the valuation processes that motivate the action.
evidence: Supported by inference from previous studies mentioned in the text

claim: Serotonin is implicated in the valuation processes that motivate action.
source: Previous studies suggested that serotonin is implicated in the motor aspects of action production and also the valuation processes that motivate the action.
evidence: Supported by inference from previous studies mentioned in the text

claim: Serotonin conditions impulse control and the capacity for behavioral inhibition.
source: Notably, serotonin was found to condition impulse control and the capacity for behavioral inhibition (Cools et al., 2005; Crockett et al., 2009; Warden et al., 2012; Guitart-Masip et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cools et al., 2005; Crockett et al., 2009; Warden et al., 2012; Guitart-Masip et al., 2014

claim: Serotonin promotes patience for delayed rewards.
source: and to promote patience for delayed rewards (Schweighofer et al., 2008; Miyazaki et al., 2014; Worbe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schweighofer et al., 2008; Miyazaki et al., 2014; Worbe et al., 2014

claim: Serotonin impacts how positive and negative outcomes guide learning in humans.
source: Serotonin also impacts the determinants of actions, for instance, how positive and negative outcomes guide learning in humans (Chamberlain et al., 2006; Crockett et al., 2009; Faulkner and Deakin, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chamberlain et al., 2006; Crockett et al., 2009; Faulkner and Deakin, 2014

claim: Serotonin impacts how positive and negative outcomes guide learning in monkeys.
source: monkeys (Clarke et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Clarke et al., 2004

claim: Serotonin impacts how positive and negative outcomes guide learning in rodents.
source: and rodents (Bari et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bari et al., 2010

claim: Serotonin regulates the impact of action costs such as punishments.
source: Key ideas are that serotonin (1) regulates the impact of action costs such as punishments (Daw et al., 2002; Niv et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Daw et al., 2002; Niv et al., 2007

claim: Serotonin regulates the impact of action costs such as delay.
source: or delay (Niv et al., 2007; Cools et al., 2011; Miyazaki et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Niv et al., 2007; Cools et al., 2011; Miyazaki et al., 2014

claim: Serotonin adjusts the propensity to activate versus inhibit action.
source: and (2) adjusts the propensity to activate versus inhibit the action (Boureau and Dayan, 2011; Cools et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boureau and Dayan, 2011; Cools et al., 2011

claim: 58 subjects were included in the analysis.
source: 58 subjects were included in the analysis, see Table 1.
evidence: Directly stated in the text

claim: Performance was significantly improved in the escitalopram group compared to the placebo group.
source: We found a significant effect of treatment group: performance was significantly improved in the escitalopram group (F1, 58.4=9.37, p=0.003) as compared to the placebo group.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The performance difference between escitalopram and placebo groups was stable over time.
source: This difference was stable over time: there was no significant interaction between groups and visits (F2, 91=0.22, p=0.8).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The average payoff per visit was £35.9±1.21 s.e.m. in the escitalopram group.
source: The average payoff per visit was £35.9±1.21 s.e.m. and £30.1±1.44 s.e.m. in the escitalopram and placebo groups respectively.
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data

claim: The average payoff per visit was £30.1±1.44 s.e.m. in the placebo group.
source: The average payoff per visit was £35.9±1.21 s.e.m. and £30.1±1.44 s.e.m. in the escitalopram and placebo groups respectively.
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data

claim: Only one model parameter (cost-evidence accumulation slope, Sem) was significantly different between the placebo and escitalopram groups.
source: Only one model parameter was significantly different between the placebo and escitalopram groups: the cost-evidence accumulation slope (Sem, F1, 58.0=9.88, p=0.003).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of computational model parameters fitted to experimental data

claim: There was a 31% decrease in cost-evidence accumulation slope (Sem) in the escitalopram group compared to the placebo group.
source: This parameter captures the average value of effort cost across conditions: there was a 31% decrease in the escitalopram group compared to the placebo group (on average with ± s.e.m., placebo: 0.16±0.012, escitalopram: 0.11±0.008)
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of experimental data

claim: The difference in cost-evidence accumulation slope between escitalopram and placebo was significant at each visit.
source: the difference was actually significant at each visit (all p<0.015; two-sided t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Effort duration was longer in the escitalopram group compared to placebo.
source: we found both a longer effort duration per se (F1, 58.1=10.72, p=0.002, on average placebo: 7.63s±0.56, escitalopram: 10.2s±0.55, with s.e.m.)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The sensitivity of effort duration to incentive level was higher in the escitalopram group compared to placebo.
source: and a higher sensitivity of effort duration to incentive level (F1, 58.5=5.46, p=0.023, on average with ± s.e.m., placebo: 1.11±0.22, escitalopram: 1.95±0.26) in the escitalopram group compared to placebo
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Effort duration and its sensitivity to incentive level are correlated across subjects.
source: The Pearson correlation over subjects was indeed significantly positive in both groups (placebo: ρ27=0.43, p=0.02; escitalopram: ρ27=0.54, p=0.002, see Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 3B

claim: Escitalopram improves global performance in a task that involves trading effort cost against monetary benefit.
source: Our behavioral results in healthy volunteers show that the SSRI escitalopram improves global performance and hence payoff in a task that involves trading effort cost against monetary benefit.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing improved payoff in escitalopram group

claim: The effect of escitalopram is characterized as a specific diminution of effort cost.
source: our computational analysis characterized the effect of escitalopram as a specific diminution of effort cost.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of experimental data

claim: Cost may be a general functional domain for serotonin.
source: Together with previous findings, our results support the hypothesis that cost may be a general functional domain for serotonin (Boureau and Dayan, 2011; Dayan, 2012).
evidence: Supported by current experimental results combined with previous literature

claim: Serotonin impacts sensitivity to negative rather than positive feedback during probabilistic and reversal learning paradigms.
source: For instance, interventions targeting serotonergic transmission during probabilistic and reversal learning paradigms in rodents, monkeys and humans suggested that serotonin impacts sensitivity to negative rather than positive feedback (Clarke et al., 2004; Chamberlain et al., 2006; Crockett et al., 2009; Bari et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clarke et al., 2004; Chamberlain et al., 2006; Crockett et al., 2009; Bari et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2015

claim: Acute tryptophan depletion reduces information sampling in a decision-making task, but only when sampling has a financial cost.
source: The reduction of serotonergic transmission in humans following acute tryptophan depletion (for a review, see Faulkner and Deakin, 2014) reduced information sampling in a decision-making task, but crucially, only when sampling had a financial cost (Crockett et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Faulkner and Deakin, 2014 and Crockett et al., 2012

claim: Serotonin may impact moral costs, such as unfairness in social decision-making.
source: Serotonin may also impact moral costs, such as unfairness in social decision-making (Crockett et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crockett et al., 2008

claim: Higher firing rate of serotonergic neurons correlates with an increased ability to wait for bigger rewards in rodents.
source: Furthermore, serotonin may control the cost of delay in reward delivery in rodents, such that a higher firing rate of serotonergic neurons correlates with an increased ability to wait for bigger rewards (Miyazaki et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyazaki et al., 2014

claim: Serotonin does not affect the sensitivity to the reward itself.
source: without affecting the sensitivity to the reward itself (Fonseca et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fonseca et al., 2015

claim: Low serotonin levels exacerbate sensitivity to the cost of waiting, which could result in impulse control disorders.
source: Conversely, low serotonin levels, e.g. after acute tryptophan depletion, were suggested to exacerbate sensitivity to the cost of waiting, which could result in impulse control disorders (Crockett et al., 2009; Cools et al., 2011; Dayan, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crockett et al., 2009; Cools et al., 2011; Dayan, 2012

claim: Serotonin blockers impacted choices only when costs were delays, and not physical efforts in cost/benefit trade-off tasks in rodents.
source: in cost/benefit trade-off tasks, serotonin blockers impacted choices only when costs were delays, and not physical efforts (Denk et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Denk et al., 2005

claim: Dopamine blockers affected both delay and physical effort costs in cost/benefit trade-off tasks in rodents.
source: whereas dopamine blockers affected both types of costs.
evidence: Inferred from context of discussion about Denk et al., 2005 study

claim: The SSRI effect on effort duration cannot be explained by a change in temporal discounting.
source: Therefore, the SSRI effect on effort duration (how long subjects sustain an effort) cannot be explained by a change in temporal discounting (how long subjects wait for a reward).
evidence: Based on logical inference from task design features

claim: Higher serotonin level alleviates the effort cost.
source: The direction of the effect obtained in the present study suggests that higher serotonin level alleviates the effort cost.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing reduced effort cost parameter with SSRI treatment

claim: The primary effect of SSRI is to increase serotonin level in the synaptic cleft.
source: This interpretation is based on the assumption that the primary effect of SSRI is to increase serotonin level in the synaptic cleft (Nutt et al., 1999; Stahl, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nutt et al., 1999; Stahl, 2008

claim: 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors respectively inhibit and excite motoneurons.
source: for instance, 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors respectively inhibit and excite motoneurons (Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992

claim: Serotonin helps overcoming delay costs in humans.
source: We nevertheless note that the superficial interpretation is consistent with demonstrations that serotonin also helps overcoming other costs such as delay in humans (Schweighofer et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schweighofer et al., 2008

claim: There was no difference in maximal force between the placebo and SSRI groups at any visit.
source: An indirect effect through an increase in muscular capacity can be excluded since there was no difference in maximal force between the placebo and SSRI groups at any visit.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Nociception and/or somatosensory perception are both modulated by serotonin at central levels.
source: The former (perceptual) view would be in line with an analgesic effect of escitalopram, which is consistent with the findings that nociception and/or somatosensory perception are both modulated by serotonin at central levels (Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992

claim: Serotonin is targeted by common drugs modulating pain like acetaminophen.
source: that serotonin is targeted by common drugs modulating pain like acetaminophen (Smith, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith, 2009

claim: Serotonin modulates the inhibitory feedback loop that allows muscular fatigue to down-regulate the motor command.
source: and that serotonin modulates the inhibitory feedback loop that allows muscular fatigue to down-regulate the motor command (Gandevia, 2001; Cotel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gandevia, 2001; Cotel et al., 2013

claim: The serotonin and dopamine systems strongly interact.
source: As the serotonin and dopamine systems strongly interact (Dremencov et al., 2009; Cools et al., 2011; Schilström et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Dremencov et al., 2009; Cools et al., 2011; Schilström et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2014

claim: Dopaminergic manipulations in mesolimbic structures affected the propensity to choose high reward – high effort over low reward – low effort options in rodents.
source: Indeed, the beneficial effect of SSRI shown here is reminiscent of previous reports about dopaminergic manipulations in mesolimbic structures, which affected the propensity to choose high reward – high effort over low reward – low effort options in rodents (Cousins et al., 1996; Salamone et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cousins et al., 1996; Salamone et al., 2007

claim: Dopaminergic manipulations in humans affect reward processing in learning contexts.
source: Indeed dopaminergic manipulations in humans have been repeatedly shown to affect reward processing, not only in learning contexts (Frank et al., 2004; Pessiglione et al., 2006; Palminteri et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Frank et al., 2004; Pessiglione et al., 2006; Palminteri et al., 2009

claim: Dopaminergic manipulations in humans affect reward processing in reward/effort trade-off paradigms.
source: but also in reward/effort trade-off paradigms (Wardle et al., 2011; Treadway et al., 2012; Le Bouc et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wardle et al., 2011; Treadway et al., 2012; Le Bouc et al., 2016

claim: Serotonin release is boosted by SSRIs from treatment onset at the molecular level.
source: However, at the molecular level, serotonin release is boosted by SSRIs from treatment onset (Kobayashi et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kobayashi et al., 2008

claim: SSRI effects on emotional processing occur with little or no delay in healthy subjects.
source: and SSRI effects on emotional processing also occur with little or no delay in healthy subjects (Harmer et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harmer et al., 2003

claim: Positive and negative outcomes can shape mood on the long run.
source: This idea has been formalized in a recent study showing how positive and negative outcomes can shape mood on the long run (Eldar and Niv, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eldar and Niv, 2015

claim: A specific modulation of cost can result in both longer efforts and an increased sensitivity of effort duration to potential benefits.
source: Finally, our results also indicate that non-trivial behavioral effects can be accounted for by a change in a single computational parameter (Sem): a specific modulation of cost can result in both longer efforts and an increased sensitivity of effort duration to potential benefits in our results.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of experimental data

claim: The task involved trading handgrip force production against monetary benefits.
source: The task involved trading handgrip force production against monetary benefits.
evidence: Direct description of experimental task design

claim: Participants in the escitalopram group produced more effort and thereby achieved a higher payoff.
source: Participants in the escitalopram group produced more effort and thereby achieved a higher payoff.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The effect of escitalopram was underpinned by a specific reduction of effort cost, and not by any change in the weight of monetary incentives.
source: Crucially, our computational analysis showed that this effect was underpinned by a specific reduction of effort cost, and not by any change in the weight of monetary incentives.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of experimental data

claim: Healthy volunteers aged 18–45 years old were recruited to the study by public advertisement.
source: Healthy volunteers (18–45 years old) were recruited to the study by public advertisement after approval by the Ethics Committee of Berkshire, UK (protocol CL1-20098-81, on 28th Sept. 2011) and registration as a clinical trial, ISRCTN75872983.
evidence: Direct description of study methodology

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Berkshire, UK on 28th Sept. 2011.
source: after approval by the Ethics Committee of Berkshire, UK (protocol CL1-20098-81, on 28th Sept. 2011)
evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval

claim: The study was registered as clinical trial ISRCTN75872983.
source: and registration as a clinical trial, ISRCTN75872983.
evidence: Direct statement of trial registration

claim: Participants gave their written informed consent prior to participation.
source: Participants gave their written informed consent prior to participation.
evidence: Direct statement of ethical procedure

claim: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two parallel treatment groups following a double-blind procedure: placebo or escitalopram.
source: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two parallel treatment groups following a double-blind procedure: placebo or escitalopram (10 mg during week #1 and #9; 20 mg from week #2 to #8).
evidence: Direct description of study methodology

claim: Escitalopram was administered at 10 mg during week #1 and #9.
source: placebo or escitalopram (10 mg during week #1 and #9; 20 mg from week #2 to #8).
evidence: Direct description of treatment protocol

claim: Escitalopram was administered at 20 mg from week #2 to #8.
source: placebo or escitalopram (10 mg during week #1 and #9; 20 mg from week #2 to #8).
evidence: Direct description of treatment protocol

claim: Participants took a daily oral capsule around 8 P.M. for 9 weeks.
source: Participants took a daily oral capsule around 8 P.M. for 9 weeks
evidence: Direct description of treatment protocol

claim: Participants performed the Effort Allocation Task three times at distinct latencies: initial (2–4 days after treatment onset), intermediate (12–17 days) and late (52–60 days).
source: and performed the Effort Allocation Task three times at distinct latencies (Figure 1B): initial (2–4 days after treatment onset), intermediate (12–17 days) and late (52–60 days for all subjects but 3, who were tested between the 33rd and 44th days before withdrawing from the study).
evidence: Direct description of study methodology, also shown in Figure 1B

claim: The maximal force was not affected by treatments.
source: The maximal force was not affected by treatments (F3, 113.7=0.93, p=0.42)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The maximal force was not affected by visits.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The maximal force was not affected by the interaction of treatment and visit factors.
source: or by the interaction of these two factors (F6, 180=0.27, p=0.95).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The same best computational model was found independently in each treatment group with high confidence levels.
source: The fact that the same best model was found independently in each treatment group with high confidence levels (exceedance probabilities xp>98% in each group) indicates that all subjects can be characterized within this common computational framework.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian model selection analysis

claim: A 20% change in any given parameter was reliably detected by the model fitting procedure in at least 77% of simulations.
source: A 20% change in any given parameter was reliably detected and the difference recovered by model fitting was significant in a 96% of simulations at least for Ai, Sem, Srm and Sri and in a 77% of simulations for Sed.
evidence: Supported by simulation analysis

claim: A change in one single parameter was recovered without propagating to other parameters and the false alarm rate was below 5% for all parameters.
source: Importantly, a change in one single parameter was recovered without propagating to other parameters and the false alarm rate was below 5% for all parameters (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by simulation analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: Models including a modulation of Sem outperformed the others in Bayesian model selection.
source: Models including a modulation of Sem outperformed the others (log Bayes Factor, all Δ>147.9), see Table 3.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian model selection analysis shown in Table 3

claim: A version with modulations of both Sem and Sed was slightly more likely than a version with only a modulation of Sem.
source: A version with modulations of both Sem and Sed was slightly more likely than a version with only a modulation of Sem (Δ=3)
evidence: Supported by Bayesian model selection analysis

claim: The model with modulations of both Sem and Sed was much more likely than any other combination.
source: and much more likely than any other combination (Δ>5.9).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian model selection analysis

claim: Serotonin regulates behavioral activation by modulating the weight of action costs rather than benefits.
source: Borrowing from these models, we retain the general working hypothesis that serotonin regulates behavioral activation by modulating the weight of action costs rather than benefits.
evidence: Stated as working hypothesis based on previous models

claim: Serotonin regulates the weight of effort cost in action production, as opposed to the weight of expected benefit.
source: Here, we tested the specific hypothesis that serotonin regulates the weight of effort cost in action production, as opposed to the weight of expected benefit.
evidence: Stated as the specific hypothesis tested in this study

claim: SSRIs might reduce the perceived cost of performing actions, which would promote behavioral activation and alleviate apathy.
source: Indeed, according to our interpretation, SSRIs might reduce the perceived cost of performing actions, which would promote behavioral activation, hence the alleviation of apathy.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental results

claim: SSRIs might reduce the perceived cost of delaying action, improving response control and reducing impulsivity.
source: As SSRIs might also reduce the perceived cost of delaying action, they would improve response control and reduce impulsivity (Cools et al., 2005; Cools et al., 2011; Crockett et al., 2009; Dayan, 2012; Bari and Robbins, 2013; Miyazaki et al., 2014; Fonseca et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental results and previous literature

claim: Serotonin and dopamine may have complementary roles in promoting action production: serotonin by reducing effort cost and dopamine by enhancing the incentive value of potential rewards.
source: It might be that serotonin and dopamine have complementary roles in promoting action production (and alleviating apathy): the former by reducing effort cost and the latter by enhancing the incentive value of potential rewards.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental results and previous literature

claim: An early detection of effort cost attenuation could be used to predict long-term treatment effects on clinical symptoms in depressed patients.
source: Further studies in depressed patients are needed to assess whether an early detection of effort cost attenuation could be used to predict long-term treatment effects on clinical symptoms.
evidence: Speculative suggestion for future research

claim: Distinct dysfunctions, such as amplification of effort cost vs. flattening of reward prospects, might call for different treatments.
source: Distinct dysfunctions, such as amplification of effort cost vs. flattening of reward prospects, might call for different treatments: if drugs modulating serotonin only affect cost estimates, then other drugs (possibly dopaminergic) should aim to impact the valuation of potential benefits.
evidence: Speculative clinical implication based on experimental results
